mainTopic: What kind of proof the recipients of a gift must bring when the giver claims he was a שכיב מרע: witnesses about his health, or only קיום השטר
overview: The משנה taught a dispute about a gift given in a שטר. The giver now says he was a שכיב מרע (deathly ill) when he gave it, while the recipients say he was healthy. רבי מאיר puts the burden of proof on the giver, and the רבנן put it on the recipients. The גמרא asks what kind of proof the recipients need. רב הונא says it means witnesses that the giver was healthy, which fits the earlier argument between רבי יעקב and רבי נתן. רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא say confirming the signatures (קיום השטר) is enough. In their view, the משנה argues about whether a שטר its writer admits writing still needs confirmation. The גמרא asks why this argument is needed when a similar one about witnesses already exists, and answers that both cases are needed. רבה agrees with the view requiring witnesses: since the deed's wording proves nothing either way, the property stays with its owner. רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש have the same argument, and רבי יוחנן begins a challenge from a story in בני ברק that continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: What kind of proof do the recipients need?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the 'proof' in the משנה means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The proof: what is it done with?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple question about the משנה. When the רבנן say the recipients must bring 'proof', what kind of proof do they mean? This sets up two different answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה never said what the proof is. It could be proof about the giver's health when he gave the gift. Or it could be proof that the שטר itself is real. Each choice changes what the whole argument is about.

phrases.english: The proof: with what is it brought?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the analysis of the משנה's word 'proof'.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of proof the recipients of the gift must bring under the view of the רבנן.

steps.title: רב הונא: The proof is through witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא says the proof means witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: the proof is with witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives the first answer. The recipients must bring witnesses who testify that the giver was healthy when he gave the gift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב הונא, the argument is about a fact: was the giver sick or healthy at that time? So the proof has to be about his health. Showing that the שטר is genuine is not enough.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
The proof is with witnesses.
phrases.notes: He means witnesses who saw that the giver was healthy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first answer to the question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The proof means witnesses who testify about the giver's health.

steps.title: רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא: The proof is confirming the deed
steps.stepSummary: A second view says the proof is only קיום השטר, confirming the signatures on the deed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא say: the proof is through confirming the שטר.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים give a different answer. The recipients do not need to prove anything about the giver's health. They only need to confirm in court that the signatures on the שטר are real.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this view, the proof is much easier to bring. Once the שטר is confirmed, the recipients win. The question is no longer about the giver's health at all. It is only about whether the document is genuine.

keyTerms.meaning: Confirming a document in court by checking that the witnesses' signatures are real

phrases.aramaic: רַב חִסְדָּא וְרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמְרִי:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna say:
The proof is with confirming the document.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חִסְדָּא וְרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמְרִי: רְאָיָה בְּקִיּוּם הַשְּׁטָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer that disagrees with רב הונא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The proof means confirming the signatures on the deed.

steps.title: For רב הונא, the dispute matches רבי יעקב and רבי נתן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that, for רב הונא, רבי מאיר and the רבנן are repeating the argument between רבי יעקב and רבי נתן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא, who said the proof is with witnesses: they argue along the lines of the argument between רבי יעקב and רבי נתן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains רב הונא's opinion. If the proof is witnesses about health, then the משנה's dispute is the same one found between רבי יעקב and רבי נתן in an earlier ברייתא. The next line tells us which side matches which.
steps.deeperAnalysis: That earlier argument asked whose side has the burden of proof about the giver's health. Do we assume his condition now shows what it was back then? Since רב הונא sees the משנה as a dispute about health, it fits right into that argument.

phrases.english: Rav Huna, who said the proof is with witnesses:
they are arguing
phrases.notes: 'They' means רבי מאיר and the רבנן of our משנה.

phrases.english: in the dispute of Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Natan.
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא brought on the previous עמוד (153b).

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רְאָיָה בְּעֵדִים – קָא מִיפַּלְגִי בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יַעֲקֹב וְרַבִּי נָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to רב הונא's answer and explains the reasoning behind it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For רב הונא, the משנה's dispute is the same as the dispute between רבי יעקב and רבי נתן.

steps.title: The memory aid: who matches whom
steps.stepSummary: Using the memory aid מניח, the גמרא matches רבי מאיר with רבי נתן and the רבנן with רבי יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: (Memory aid: מניח.) רבי מאיר follows רבי נתן, and the רבנן follow רבי יעקב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a short memory aid. It then pairs each side of our משנה with one side of the earlier argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי נתן holds that we assume the giver's condition now reflects his condition then. So a giver who is healthy now must prove he was sick, just as רבי מאיר says. The רבנן put the burden on the recipients, which matches רבי יעקב.

keyTerms.meaning: In line with, following the view of

steps.whatToRemember: For רב הונא, the proof is witnesses about health. In this view, רבי מאיר follows רבי נתן and the רבנן follow רבי יעקב.

phrases.english: (Memory aid: Manniach.)
phrases.notes: The letters מ-נ-י-ח stand for מאיר, נתן, יעקב, חכמים. The first two go together, and so do the last two.

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Natan,
and the Rabbis follow Rabbi Yaakov.

steps.triggerLanguage: סִימָן: מַנִּיחַ. רַבִּי מֵאִיר – כְּרַבִּי נָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רב הונא's explanation by showing which side matches which.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר follows רבי נתן; the רבנן follow רבי יעקב.

steps.title: For רב חסדא, the dispute is about a person who admits he wrote a deed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that, for רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא, the argument is whether a שטר the signer admits writing still needs confirmation in court.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא, who said the proof is by confirming the שטר: they argue about whether someone who admits he wrote a document still needs it confirmed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains the second view. In this view, the משנה's dispute is a well-known question: if a person admits he wrote a שטר, must it still be confirmed in court? The next lines give each side's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the giver admits he wrote the gift שטר. He only claims he was sick at the time. So the whole case turns on how strong a שטר is when its writer admits it is his.

keyTerms.meaning: To have it confirmed in court

phrases.aramaic: רַב חִסְדָּא וְרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמְרִי
phrases.english: Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna, who say
the proof is with confirming the document:
they argue about one who admits to a document
that he wrote it: must it be confirmed?

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חִסְדָּא וְרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמְרִי רְאָיָה בְּקִיּוּם הַשְּׁטָר – קָא מִיפַּלְגִי בְּמוֹדֶה בִּשְׁטָר שֶׁכְּתָבוֹ צָרִיךְ לְקַיְּימוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the second answer (step 3) and explains its reasoning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For רב חסדא, the משנה's dispute is whether a שטר that its writer admits writing still needs קיום.

steps.title: Each side's position on a deed its writer admits
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר says no confirmation is needed. The רבנן say confirmation is still needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר holds that one who admits he wrote a שטר does not need it confirmed. The רבנן hold that even then it must be confirmed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the two sides. רבי מאיר says the giver's admission makes the שטר valid without checking. The רבנן say it must still be confirmed in court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי מאיר, the שטר already stands, so the giver must prove he was sick. For the רבנן, the recipients must first confirm the שטר. That confirmation is the 'proof' the משנה means, and once it is done they win.
steps.whatToRemember: For רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא, the proof is only קיום השטר. רבי מאיר holds a deed its writer admits needs no confirmation, so the giver must prove he was sick. The רבנן require confirmation, so the recipients must confirm the deed.
steps.confusionAlert: In this view, the recipients do not need to prove the giver was healthy. They only confirm the signatures, and that alone wins the case.

phrases.english: For Rabbi Meir holds:
one who admits to a document that he wrote it
does not need to have it confirmed.
And the Rabbis hold:
one who admits to a document that he wrote it
needs to have it confirmed.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר סָבַר: מוֹדֶה בִּשְׁטָר שֶׁכְּתָבוֹ – אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ לְקַיְּימוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the two positions in the dispute introduced in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: no קיום is needed when the writer admits the שטר. רבנן: קיום is still needed.

steps.title: Didn't they already argue about this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the need for the argument between רבי מאיר and the רבנן, since a ברייתא already shows them arguing about a very similar case.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't they already argue about this once? A ברייתא teaches: witnesses are not believed to cancel the document. That is רבי מאיר's view. The חכמים say they are believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why we need the argument from Step 7 at all. רבי מאיר and the חכמים already argue about something similar in a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, witnesses confirm their own signatures but say they were unfit to sign. רבי מאיר says they cannot cancel the שטר, and the חכמים say they can. That looks like the same idea as Step 7: someone stands behind a document and then tries to cancel it. So the second argument seems repetitive.

phrases.english: But didn't they already argue about this once?
As it is taught in a ברייתא:
They are not believed to make it invalid,
phrases.notes: This is about witnesses who confirm their signatures on a שטר but then say they were unfit to sign.

phrases.english: these are the words of רבי מאיר.
And the חכמים say: they are believed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the argument laid out in Step 7
steps.kashyaTarget: The argument between רבי מאיר and the רבנן about a שטר the signer admits writing
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same two תנאים already argue about witnesses who try to cancel a document they confirmed, so the second argument seems to teach nothing new.

steps.title: Both arguments are needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers צריכא. Each argument teaches something the other could not teach.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is necessary. If only the witnesses' case were taught, I would think the רבנן say so only there, because witnesses are powerful and can weaken a document. But here, where it is not in the giver's power, I would say no. And if only this case were taught, I would think רבי מאיר says so only here. But in the witnesses' case I would say he agrees with the רבנן. So both are necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that we need both arguments. From either one alone we could have guessed wrong about the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From the witnesses' case alone, we might think the רבנן believe the witnesses only because witnesses have special power to weaken a שטר. A giver has no such power. From the giver's case alone, we might think רבי מאיר rejects only the giver. He might agree that witnesses can cancel. Each case blocks a different wrong guess.

keyTerms.meaning: it is necessary (to teach both cases)
it is not in his power

steps.whatToRemember: Both arguments are needed. רבי מאיר keeps his view even about witnesses, and the רבנן keep theirs even about the giver who admits he wrote the שטר.

phrases.english: It is necessary, because if only that one were taught,
phrases.notes: "That one" is the witnesses' case from the ברייתא in Step 8.

phrases.english: I would think the רבנן say it only in that case,
because witnesses are powerful and can weaken the document;

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא – הוּא דְּלָאו כָּל כְּמִינֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: but here, with him, where it is not in his power,
phrases.notes: "Him" is the giver who admits he wrote the שטר.

phrases.english: I would say they do not believe him;
and if it were taught only in this case,
I would think רבי מאיר says it only in this case;

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּהָךְ, אֵימָא מוֹדֶה לְהוּ לְרַבָּנַן;
phrases.english: but in that case, I would say he agrees with the רבנן;
So it is necessary.

steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: each case teaches something the other cannot
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each argument alone could have been limited to its own case, because of the special power of witnesses or the special weakness of the giver.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both arguments are needed. רבי מאיר holds his view even about witnesses, and the רבנן hold theirs even about the giver.

steps.title: רבה: the proof is by witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that the ראיה the recipients must bring means witnesses that the giver was healthy.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so said רבה: the proof is by witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה takes a side on the question from earlier steps: what kind of proof is needed? He says it means real witnesses about the giver's health, not just confirming the signatures.
steps.deeperAnalysis: וכן means 'and so too'. רבה sides with רב הונא from Step 2, against the view in Step 3 that the proof is only קיום השטר. The recipients must bring עדים who testify that the giver was healthy when he gave the gift.

phrases.english: And so said רבה:
The proof is by witnesses.
phrases.notes: He means witnesses who saw the giver was healthy, not just people who confirm the signatures.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the question of what kind of ראיה is needed, and agrees with רב הונא (Step 2) that it means witnesses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The recipients' proof must be witnesses that the giver was healthy.

steps.title: אביי: the missing wording cuts both ways
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks for רבה's reason. A missing 'healthy' phrase cannot prove the giver was sick, because the 'sick' phrase is also missing.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: What is the reason? If you say that every deed writes 'when he was walking on his feet in the marketplace,' and this one does not, so he must have been a שכיב מרע: on the contrary! Every deed of a sick man writes 'when he was sick and lying in his bed,' and this one does not, so he must have been healthy!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רבה. He asks why the recipients should need witnesses at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One could say the deed looks suspicious because it lacks the usual line for a healthy giver. אביי answers that it also lacks the usual line for a sick giver. So the missing wording proves nothing either way. אביי is attacking the reason someone might give for רבה's rule.
steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not saying the giver was healthy. He is showing that the argument from missing wording works both ways, so it proves nothing.

phrases.english: אביי said to him: What is the reason?
If we say: since in all of them it is written,
phrases.notes: "All of them" means all regular gift deeds of a healthy person.

phrases.english: "When he was walking on his feet in the marketplace,"
and in this one it is not written,
learn from this that he was a person on his deathbed;
On the contrary!
Since in all of them it is written,
phrases.notes: Here "all of them" means deeds of a sick person.

phrases.english: "When he was sick and lying in his bed,"
and in this one it is not written,
learn from this that he was healthy!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason behind רבה's ruling in Step 10
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's rule that the recipients need witnesses that the giver was healthy
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The deed lacks the 'healthy' wording, but it also lacks the 'sick' wording. So the missing wording cannot make the deed suspicious enough to need witnesses.

steps.title: רבה answers: the document is silent, so the property stays with the owner
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers אביי. Since the document can be read either way, nothing is proven from it, and the property stays with its owner's side.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can say it this way, and you can say it that way. So leave the money in the hands of its owner.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers אביי's question. The document proves nothing either way, so we fall back on leaving the property with its owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי had pointed out that the document is missing both the 'healthy' wording and the 'sick' wording. רבה agrees, and that is exactly his point: the document is useless as proof. When things are unclear, the property stays with its last known owner, the giver, who is the one now claiming he was a שכיב מרע. So the recipients must bring witnesses that he was healthy.

keyTerms.meaning: One can say it this way
Leave the money where it is
In the hands of its owner

phrases.aramaic: אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר הָכִי וְאִיכָּא לְמֵימַר הָכִי,
phrases.english: One can say this, and one can say that,
phrases.notes: He means the document can be read as 'healthy' or as 'sick'. It doesn't settle anything.

phrases.english: so establish the property in the possession of its owner.
phrases.notes: The owner is the giver himself, who says he was sick. So the recipients are the ones who must prove their claim.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר הָכִי וְאִיכָּא לְמֵימַר הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question from step 11 by agreeing the document is silent and using that to explain the ruling.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Turns the question into the reason: since the document proves nothing, ownership stays where it was.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אביי thought the missing 'healthy' wording could not be a reason to require witnesses.
steps.terutzMaskana: Exactly because nothing can be learned from the document, the property stays with the owner, and the recipients need witnesses.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש argue about what proof means
steps.stepSummary: The same question, what kind of proof the recipients must bring, is an argument between רבי יוחנן (witnesses) and רבי שמעון בן לקיש (confirming the document).
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is an argument between אמוראים. רבי יוחנן says: the proof is with witnesses. רבי שמעון בן לקיש says: the proof is by confirming the document.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the question of what 'proof' means, which רבה answered with 'witnesses', is also argued by two other great אמוראים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן agrees with רבה: the recipients need witnesses that the giver was healthy. רבי שמעון בן לקיש says it is enough to confirm that the document is real, which is called קיום השטר. On his view, once the document is shown to be real, the gift holds.

keyTerms.meaning: Confirming that a document is real, by checking the signatures

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the coming objection. רבי יוחנן will try to prove from a ברייתא that confirming the document is not enough.

phrases.english: And it is the subject of a dispute;
for Rabbi Yochanan says: the proof is through witnesses,
and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says:
the proof is through confirming the document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that רבה's explanation of 'proof' matches one side of an argument between אמוראים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן: the recipients must bring witnesses. רבי שמעון בן לקיש: confirming the document is enough.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן challenges ריש לקיש with the story from בני ברק
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן brings a ברייתא against רבי שמעון בן לקיש. In בני ברק, a man sold his father's property and died. His relatives claimed he was a minor, so the sale was not valid. רבי עקיבא refused to allow digging up the body to check.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן challenged רבי שמעון בן לקיש: There was a case in בני ברק. A man sold some of his father's property and then died. His family members came and protested, saying: he was a minor when he died. They came and asked רבי עקיבא: may we examine the body? He said to them: you are not allowed to disgrace him. And also, the signs of adulthood can change after death.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן starts a challenge against רבי שמעון בן לקיש by telling a story from a ברייתא. The גמרא is setting up the challenge here, and its point continues on the next עמוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The family says the sale was not valid because the seller was a minor. רבי עקיבא rules that the body may not be dug up, for two reasons: it disgraces the dead, and the body's signs of adulthood change after death anyway. So the question becomes who must prove the seller's age, and how. רבי יוחנן will use this to show that a valid document alone is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: They protested, they challenged the sale
A minor, not yet an adult, whose sale of inherited land is not valid
To disgrace him (by digging up and examining his body)

steps.confusionAlert: The story is not finished on this עמוד. רבי עקיבא's answer only explains why they cannot check the body. The part of the ברייתא that actually challenges רבי שמעון בן לקיש continues on the next עמוד.

phrases.aramaic: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan raised an objection to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish:
There was an incident in Bnei Brak
involving one who sold some of his father's property, and died,
and family members came and contested the sale,
saying: he was a minor at the time of his death,
and they came and asked Rabbi Akiva:
May we examine him?
phrases.notes: They mean digging up the body to check for signs of adulthood.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: אִי אַתֶּם רַשָּׁאִים לְנַוְּולוֹ.
phrases.english: He said to them: you are not permitted to disgrace him.

phrases.aramaic: וְעוֹד, סִימָנִין עֲשׂוּיִין לְהִשְׁתַּנּוֹת לְאַחַר מִיתָה.
phrases.english: And furthermore, signs of adulthood tend to change after death.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי יוחנן attacks the opposing view from step 13 using a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמעון בן לקיש's view that confirming the document is enough proof.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The case in the ברייתא is about whether the seller was a minor, which a real document cannot answer. This sets up the argument, which continues on the next עמוד, that proof must be about the facts behind the document.
